authority.legal_name: British Columbia Ferry Services Inc. (BC Ferries), operating the regulated coastal ferry system under the Coastal Ferry Act, overseen by the BC Ferry Commissioner
authority.geography_type: a sheltered inland sea (the Salish Sea) of deep straits, tidal passes and an archipelago of islands between the mainland and Vancouver Island
authority.home_waters_label: the Salish Sea and British Columbia's south coast

mandate.summary: BC Ferries operates British Columbia's coastal ferry network as a regulated essential public service, connecting coastal and island communities across 47 terminals and dozens of routes. Its mandate is safe, reliable, affordable service and, increasingly, decarbonization of a diesel fleet under provincial climate law.
current_priorities: Fleet renewal and decarbonization under the Clean Futures Plan (2022) — battery-hybrid-electric Island Class vessels and terminal electrification
Meeting CleanBC-mandated emissions targets for a system that is a large single source of provincial marine emissions
Improving reliability and reducing crossing times on congested core corridors between Metro Vancouver, Victoria, Nanaimo and the Gulf Islands

policy_targets.interim_target: At least 27% reduction in greenhouse-gas emissions from a 2008 baseline by 2030, mandated under the provincial CleanBC plan
policy_targets.vision: CleanBC (province-wide climate plan) and BC Ferries' own Clean Futures Plan (2022) — a staged path from diesel to battery-hybrid to all-electric vessels and electrified terminals, toward net zero by 2050
policy_targets.relevance: A zero-emission, foiling fast-passenger tier advances the 2030 CleanBC target and the 2050 net-zero goal directly, while adding faster downtown-to-downtown passenger crossings that the vehicle-ferry fleet cannot serve.

precedent.headline: BC Ferries has already committed capital to a zero-emission coastal fleet.

existing_fleet_program.operator: BC Ferries (British Columbia Ferry Services Inc.)
existing_fleet_program.vessels: Six battery-hybrid-electric Island Class vessels in service, engineered to convert to all-electric as terminal charging is built; associated terminal electrification underway
existing_fleet_program.proof_stat: Island Class electrification is projected to cut roughly 10,000 tonnes CO2e per year, supporting the Province's CleanBC targets
existing_fleet_program.note: Establishes that BC Ferries treats zero-emission propulsion as core fleet strategy, not a pilot — the foiling passenger tier extends that commitment to fast passenger service.

fast_passenger_gap.detail: British Columbia has repeatedly sought fast downtown-to-downtown passenger links (Vancouver-Victoria, Vancouver-Nanaimo) that vehicle ferries and past fast-cat experiments could not sustain economically or quietly.
fast_passenger_gap.relevance: A hydrofoiling passenger vessel — 10x more efficient than a planing fast-cat, low-wake and near-silent — is the missing technology that makes fast passenger service viable without the wake and fuel penalties that ended earlier attempts.

interpretation_for_navier: Navier is not proposing a novelty for British Columbia. BC Ferries already runs a zero-emission fleet program and the province already mandates deep marine-emission cuts. What is missing is a fast, low-wake, zero-emission passenger tier above the vehicle-ferry network — downtown Vancouver to downtown Victoria and Nanaimo, and quiet connectors across the Gulf Islands — that advances CleanBC targets while serving trips the car-ferry fleet cannot.

domestic_network.note: Candidate boarding points with APPROXIMATE anchor coordinates [lng, lat]. Precise berths and routed geometry are Grok's to seal. Coordinates are anchor-grade, not survey-grade.

domestic_pairs.rationale: The marquee corridor: downtown Vancouver to downtown Victoria, city-centre to city-centre. A zero-emission foiling passenger vessel serves this end-to-end faster than the drive-plus-ferry, with no wake penalty. Route entirely on open Salish Sea water.
Downtown Vancouver to downtown Nanaimo fast passenger — the corridor earlier fast-ferry attempts targeted; foiling makes it quiet and efficient enough to sustain.
The core Metro Vancouver to Greater Victoria ferry corridor; a passenger foiling tier relieves peak vehicle-ferry demand and cuts crossing time.
West Vancouver to Nanaimo across the Strait of Georgia; a fast passenger overlay on a congested core route.
Short Sunshine Coast connector; foiling cuts the crossing and serves commuters into Metro Vancouver quietly.
Greater Victoria to Salt Spring Island via Satellite Channel; connects the largest Gulf Island to the regional network.
Intra-Salt Spring connector between the two main harbours; quiet foiling ideal for a sensitive island community.
Inter-island Gulf Islands connector (Salt Spring to Mayne) through the archipelago; must route clear of Active Pass traffic.

regional_links.note: Secondary and clearly optional; the case stands on the domestic BC coast network. Cross-border US links are a later option, not the headline.

links.note: Mirrors the historic Victoria-Seattle passenger corridor across the Strait of Juan de Fuca / Haro Strait. International; requires customs and is explicitly out of scope for phase 1.

routing_hazards.instruction: Every domestic leg must be routed through navigable open water only — no land crossings, no crossing the Saanich or Vancouver Island landmasses, no shortcuts across islands. Provide explicit hand waypoints at each pinch point.

hazards.detail: The narrow, high-current channel between Galiano and Mayne Islands carries heavy vehicle-ferry traffic. Gulf Islands legs must route around it or transit with explicit traffic-aware waypoints; never cut across the islands.

Vancouver Harbour's entrance under the Lions Gate Bridge is a narrow tidal gate. Any Vancouver Harbour departure must exit through First Narrows into English Bay before crossing the Strait of Georgia.
The narrow channel between Vancouver Island and Salt Spring Island; Fulford / Cowichan-area legs must follow the channel, not cross land.
Vancouver-Nanaimo and Vancouver-Victoria legs cross open, weather-exposed water with commercial shipping lanes near Roberts Bank; route mid-channel clear of the Tsawwassen traffic-separation scheme.
Dense islands, reefs and shoals between Vancouver Island and the mainland; every inter-island leg must stay in charted navigable channels with hand waypoints, never straight-line across islands.
